analysis.one_liner: Requires TV-recording and video-conversion devices to obey studio copy-restriction signals and delete blocked recordings.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by the House Judiciary chairman with a Democratic cosponsor, never received a hearing or vote and died when the Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every device that converts or records analog video — TV tuners, capture cards, recorders — to detect embedded 'copy prohibited' or 'copy once' signals and obey them. Devices would have to destroy any recording flagged as copy-prohibited within 90 minutes, refuse to pass protected content to unprotected outputs, and block sale of tools that modify or defeat these controls. The government's patent office would certify which technologies count and could enforce improvements to the required watermark system. Violators would face lawsuits, damages of $200 to $2,500 per device, and criminal penalties up to five years in prison and $500,000 in fines for commercial violations.
analysis.who_benefits: Movie studios, television networks, and cable and satellite content owners. The bill would give them a legally enforceable way to restrict what viewers can record and share, backed by private lawsuits, statutory damages, impoundment of devices, and federal criminal prosecution of commercial circumvention.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Movie studios and TV content owners

how_it_helps.text: Bans manufacturing, importing, or selling any analog video device that does not detect and obey the CGMS-A and VEIL copy-control signaling system, conforming recording and redistribution to the rights encoded in the signal [S2][S3].
Requires devices to destroy copy-prohibited content within 90 minutes of receipt, and to route any permitted recordings through government-certified protected methods [S3].

Gives content owners a private right of action with injunctions, device impoundment, statutory damages of $200–$2,500 per device (tripled for repeat violations), plus criminal penalties of up to $500,000 and five years for commercial violations [S3].

Directs the Patent and Trademark Office to certify covered formats, output and recording technologies, and to adopt improvements to the VEIL watermark so the rights-signaling system stays effective [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary consumers and the companies that build their devices. Viewers would lose the ability to freely record and keep broadcasts and pay-TV content, recorders would self-delete flagged content after 90 minutes, and manufacturers would bear compliance costs and litigation exposure — costs likely passed into device prices. Libraries, archives, schools, and public broadcasters would gain narrow protections but still face civil liability.
analysis.who_pays_short: Consumers, electronics makers, and PC makers

drawbacks.text: The bill mandates that recorders automatically destroy copy-flagged content after 90 minutes and bars passing protected content to unprotected outputs, restricting what people can do with programs received over the air or on discs they lawfully receive [S3].

It writes a specific proprietary watermark technology (VEIL) into federal law and empowers the Patent and Trademark Office to adjust its detection function, giving a private technology a government-mandated role in every covered device [S3].

Broad liability — statutory damages per device plus bans on trafficking in tools that modify or defeat compliance — could chill device innovation and expose makers of general-purpose equipment, with relief only through exceptions for pre-existing and display-only devices [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's legitimate aim — stopping commercial-scale piracy of movies and TV — is served by its criminal penalties and its ban on trafficking in defeat devices. But the mechanism reaches far past counterfeiters into ordinary home recording: it would have constrained every consumer recorder, mandated self-deleting recordings, and given content owners sweeping lawsuit rights over device design. Its carve-outs for libraries and education, and its graduated copy rules (one free copy of many broadcasts), soften but do not remove the cost to ordinary users.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in December 2005 by the House Judiciary chairman, it was referred to the Judiciary Committee and then to its courts and intellectual property subcommittee in February 2006, and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Sensenbrenner (R-WI), the House Judiciary chairman, introduced the bill with Rep. Conyers (D-MI) on December 16, 2005; it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the same day [S3][S5].
On February 16, 2006, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Courts, the Internet, and Intellectual Property; no further action is recorded for the remainder of the 109th Congress [S5].

The bill proposed banning the manufacture, import, or sale of analog video conversion and recording devices unless they honor embedded copy-control signals, and imposed civil and criminal penalties for violations [S2][S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers and consumer-electronics and PC makers are better off because the bill died: recorders kept working as they always had and no self-deletion mandate or new liability regime took effect. Content owners did not obtain the mandated copy-control regime through this bill.

for.name: F. James Sensenbrenner Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and made introductory remarks on the House floor the day after referral [S3][S5].

for.name: Movie and television content owners (Motion Picture Association)
for.what_they_did: Backed mandatory analog copy-control legislation closing the 'analog hole'; the bill's signaling scheme and business-model rules mirror the industry's proposals.

against.name: House Judiciary Subcommittee on Courts, the Internet, and Intellectual Property
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on February 16, 2006 and never held a markup or advanced the bill [S5].

against.name: Public interest and consumer technology groups
against.role: Public Knowledge and allied consumer advocates
against.what_they_did: Criticized the bill as mandating copy controls in ordinary home devices and restricting lawful personal recording, opposing its passage.

against.name: Consumer electronics and PC manufacturers
against.role: Makers of TVs, recorders, tuners, and computers
against.what_they_did: Opposed mandates requiring redesign of every analog video device around government-certified copy-control technology.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — the Republican committee chairman introduced it with a senior Democrat as cosponsor, and the bill's life and death tracked industry positions rather than party lines; no floor vote ever split the chambers.

industries.industry: Movie studios and TV content owners
industries.note: The bill would make their copy-control signals legally binding in every consumer recorder, with private lawsuits, per-device damages, and criminal penalties behind them. The cost of enforcement would fall on viewers' ability to record and keep programming they receive.

They would bear the cost of redesigning tuners, capture cards, and recorders around certified protection technologies, and face lawsuits and impoundment for noncompliance. Their interest in blocking the bill ran alongside consumers' interest in unrestricted devices.

industries.industry: Holder of the VEIL watermark technology
industries.note: The bill writes the VEIL invisible-light watermark into federal law, requires it in covered devices, and has the Patent and Trademark Office maintain and improve it — making a private technology a mandatory component consumers pay for in every device.

industries.industry: Libraries, archives, schools, and public broadcasters
industries.note: The bill exempts them from criminal penalties and requires courts to remit damages where they acted unknowingly, but they would still face civil liability and the device mandates if they trafficked in covered equipment.
